title: Replica Transition at Measurement-Altered Ising Criticality
authors: Kabir Khanna, Sara Murciano, Romain Vasseur
abstract: Performing measurements on gapless quantum ground states can give rise to new universal phenomena, whose origins remain poorly understood even for the paradigmatic Ising critical point. Replica methods offer a natural framework to study such post-measurement ensembles, with the replica limit $Q\to 1$ describing physical Born-averaged observables. Here we show that, for the monitored critical Ising chain, the replicated post-measurement ensemble of states itself undergoes a phase transition precisely at the physically relevant replica limit $Q \to 1$, preventing standard replica treatments. We use boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) methods to explain the underlying mechanism of this transition. Our methods yield a perturbative analytic calculation of the universal $O(1)$ constant in the Shannon entropy of the measurement record, previously known only numerically. We also apply our tools to study measurement-averaged spin correlators, providing a unified description of the universal properties of measurement outcomes and post-measurement states in the critical Ising chain.
summary: This paper analyzes the universal physics arising from measuring gapless quantum ground states, focusing on the critical Ising chain. It reveals that the replicated ensemble itself undergoes a phase transition exactly at the physical limit ($Q=1$), which standard methods fail to capture. By employing Boundary Conformal Field Theory, the authors analytically calculate key universal quantities, providing a unified description of measurement outcomes and post-measurement states.
main_problem: The paper investigates universal phenomena arising from performing measurements on gapless quantum ground states, specifically focusing on a phase transition within the replicated post-measurement ensemble itself.
main_result: The replicated post-measurement ensemble undergoes a phase transition precisely at the physically relevant replica limit $Q 	o 1$, which is explained using Boundary Conformal Field Theory (BCFT). The authors provide an analytic calculation for the universal constant in the Shannon entropy of the measurement record.
method: The primary methods involve replica techniques combined with Boundary Conformal Field Theory (BCFT) to analyze the effective action governing the replica flow. Calculations utilize generating functions and perturbative expansions in the replica parameter $Q$.
model_or_system: The system studied is the critical Ising chain, modeled by the $c=1/2$ Ising Conformal Field Theory (CFT). Measurements are modeled as weak coupling ($\gamma$) to the spin field $\sigma(x)$ on the ground state $|\psi_0angle$.
key_observables: Replicated Born Weight ($p_Q^m$), R\'enyi entropy ($R(Q)$), Shannon entropy ($S$), and measurement-averaged spin correlators ($C_k(x)$).
important_parameters: Replica number $Q$ (especially the limit $Q 	o 1$), measurement strength $\gamma$, and the effective boundary condition parameter $\lambda$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the validity of replica methods near the critical point, despite the transition occurring at the physical limit $Q=1$. Calculations often rely on continuum limits and isolating universal $\mathcal{O}(1)$ contributions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the replica phase diagram, showing the singularity at $Q^*=1$. Other figures detail the evaluation of universal constants derived from the BCC operator expansion.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of measurement-induced criticality and the failure of standard replica treatments at $Q=1$. It then employs BCFT to analyze the replica transition, deriving the universal constant for the Shannon entropy. Finally, it extends these tools to calculate higher-order measurement-averaged spin correlators.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep theoretical understanding of how measurement back-action modifies critical quantum systems, using advanced CFT techniques to calculate universal quantities previously only known numerically. This methodology is highly relevant for understanding quantum measurement processes in many-body systems.
